title: How I learned to stop worrying and love StopGrads: Stationarity, Convergence, and a case study on Flow Map Learning
claim: Updates that are not true gradients can still converge to the desired minimum, but some can instead drift to limit cycles.
layout: Left Escher-style image pair; right 3 vector-field panels with shared legend
description: The left side shows two engraving-style images side by side. One is a mountain valley with a hiker, standing for gradient landscapes. The other is an Escher-like impossible staircase scene, standing for update fields that make no progress. The right side has three square panels with blue backgrounds and gray streamlines. Panel (a) is a radial gradient field. Its trajectory runs straight from a red start dot to a black star at the minimum, labeled g=∇L. Panel (b) is a swirling non-gradient field. Its curved trajectory still ends at the star. Panel (c) is a spiral field with a hollow star as an unstable point. The trajectory leaves the minimum and goes to a dashed attracting limit cycle. A shared legend marks stable and unstable points, the limit cycle and the trajectory start. A purple-to-yellow colorbar shows time. The eye goes first to the Escher art, then to the colorful trajectories.
caption: Gradient and non-gradient update fields. Left: Gradient fields are familiar valleys and mountains, while in stopgrad update fields, learning can make no progress and may not converge (Relativity, M.C. Escher). Right: (a) A well-behaved gradient field. (b, c) Non-gradient fields can result from stopgrads. While (b) still has a stable stationary point at the minimum, (c) has an unstable stationary point; small perturbations move trajectories away from the minimum and toward the limit cycle. In this work, we study a class of loss functions and stopgrad placements that yield update fields that converge to desired stationary points.
abstract: Stopgrads are widely used in training machine learning models, but stopgrads can alter the gradient, stationary points and convergence guarantees of the original objective, which can make stopgrad training theoretically ungrounded. We introduce a stopgrad regression principle, which identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of stationary points and their uniqueness, unifying stopgrad objectives for flow maps, reinforcement learning, and diffusion samplers. We provide theoretical grounding for optimizing stopgrad flow map objectives by showing their unique stationary point is the true flow map, and showing positive convergence results for Eulerian and Lagrangian objectives, including MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow. Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map has a closed-form expression composing the initial flow map and the true flow map. We additionally use our stopgrad regression principle to propose modified stopgrad placements for flow map objectives which reduce training memory by 2x.
